extracted.intended_audience: researchers and students in humor studies, cognitive psychology, linguistics/semiotics, and scholars interested in cartoon design and reception (also relevant to cartoonists interested in cognitive constraints on humor)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating how pocket cartoons are perceived (funny or not) using cognitive and demographic predictors, especially the cartoon's mentalizing complexity, topical content, and publication date. The study uses pairwise forced-choice ratings from museum visitors to relate cartoon features to audience preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mentalizing level (number of mindstates)
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of actively engaged characters in the cartoon plus an additional level for the viewer; this mentalizing level determines how demanding the cartoon is of the viewer’s mindreading (theory-of-mind) capacities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentalizing was assessed following Dunbar et al. (2016): count actively engaged characters (a crowd counts as one level if integral to the joke) and add one for the observer. Examples: two characters conversing = third order (two characters + viewer); cartoons were assigned 2–4 in this sample. Prior work shows very high inter-rater agreement (~98%, never more than one mindstate different).

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper limit on mentalizing (cartoons)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an upper limit on how many mindstates a cartoon can successfully include before appreciation declines — for pocket (single-panel) cartoons this limit is lower than for verbal jokes (about third order intentionality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cartoons in the sample ranged 2–4 (mean ≈ 2.82), significantly lower than verbal jokes (mean ≈ 4.27). Appreciation increases with mentalizing up to a point, then declines when the required mentalizing exceeds typical adult capacities; single-panel, 2D format appears to impose this tighter limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cartoon topic categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify cartoons into topic types when evaluating or comparing them: Domestic dynamics; Social commentary; Political commentary; Verbal jokes; Visual jokes; Situational jokes/slapstick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each category has a functional definition and examples (e.g., Domestic dynamics = marital/romantic relationship jokes; Visual jokes = humor from juxtaposition/metaphor often with no text). Categories overlap; authors chose six rather than previous four-category taxonomies to better capture variety. Topic classification used in analyses of preferences and mentalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication date / recency
rubrics_metrics.description: The date of original publication influences contemporary audience preference; more recent cartoons are generally preferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Difference in publication date between paired cartoons was a significant predictor of preference (more recent cartoon usually preferred). Political jokes are especially time-sensitive and reflect historical/contextual knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual multimodality (text vs pure visual)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a cartoon contains text (speech bubbles, captions) or is purely visual affects comprehensibility and how information for the joke is conveyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most pocket cartoons are multimodal, with text providing key contextual cues; purely visual cartoons (13% in sample) can work but often require signposting/labels. Unlabeled drawings are open to multiple interpretations and may need verbal cues to guide the reader to the intended punchline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience background knowledge / familiarity
rubrics_metrics.description: A viewer's familiarity with the butt of the joke, relevant social/political context, and historical allusions is necessary for successful comprehension, especially for political cartoons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political cartoons may demand considerable background knowledge; lack of topic familiarity reduces amusement. Designers/evaluators should consider how much external knowledge is required to resolve the incongruity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate recognizability / time-depth constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Pocket cartoons typically need to be 'gotten' straight away; if the viewer does not immediately recognize and resolve the incongruity, the cartoon is rarely amusing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single-panel cartoons encapsulate a storyline in compressed form with minimal time for reflection; successful cartoons build expectations and resolve them quickly. This argues for clarity and efficient signposting in cartoon design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural mentalizing difference vs oral jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike oral jokes (which include the speaker’s mindstate as a structural level), cartoons lack a visible intermediary comedian, which changes the counting of structural mindstates and the cognitive dynamics of appreciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the artist is absent as an intermediary, cartoons may free up one structural mentalizing level compared to oral jokes; however, pictorial constraints often prevent exploiting that spare level to increase complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signposting / labels within cartoons
rubrics_metrics.description: In-cartoon signposting (labels or brief identifiers) is a useful device to provide context and guide the viewer toward the intended interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Of the purely visual cartoons sampled, some used labels to provide context; authors note that some high-order mentalizing tasks in cartoon form required verbal labeling to point observers to the intended reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic temporal sensitivity (fashionability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some cartoon topics are more tied to the contemporary moment (fashionable/time-sensitive) and thus less likely to be appreciated across time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political jokes are especially time-dependent and are less appreciated when older; social, domestic, and visual jokes are more immune to fashion effects and tend to endure better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender differences in audience preference
rubrics_metrics.description: Male and female viewers show systematic, if modest, differences in topic preference and possibly in how they weight types of humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this sample women preferred social and political commentary and domestic topics slightly more, whereas men preferred situational/slapstick and visual jokes more; overall agreement between genders was high (r = 0.948), but some pairings/topics showed significant gender divergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mentalizing scoring conventions (coding rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit coding conventions for assigning mentalizing levels to cartoons (e.g., how to count crowds, whether passive/background characters count) are necessary for reliable measurement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors counted a crowd as a single mentalizing level if it was part of the joke, excluded non-engaged/background characters, and added one level for the viewer. Prior studies show high reliability under these conventions; disagreements typically within one mindstate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-panel 2D format constraint on complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: The single-panel, two-dimensional nature of pocket cartoons constrains the cartoonist’s ability to represent multiple interacting mindstates and events, limiting achievable complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors’ attempts to render high-order mentalizing tasks as single-panel cartoons failed beyond fourth order; representing many characters and interactions without time depth is challenging and often leads cartoonists to rely on simpler mentalizing structures or textual cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pairwise forced-choice preference measurement (evaluation method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluating cartoon funniness via pairwise forced-choice (which of two cartoons is funnier) is an efficient method for public exhibition settings and yields summed preference proportions for analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to minimize participant burden: participants pick which of a paired A/B set is funnier; analysis uses proportion preferring A as dependent variable with predictors such as difference in mentalizing, gender, age, and publication date. Useful where quick, low-load measurement is required.
